newsitem.title: USA: Government rejects Staples-Office Depot merger.
newsitem.headline: Government rejects Staples-Office Depot merger.

text.p: A government agency voted Monday to ask a federal judge to halt the proposed $4 billion merger of Staples Inc. and Office Depot Inc., saying it would raise prices to consumers.
The news sent Office Depot's stock skidding about 23 percent as it lost $5.25 to $17.375 in afternoon trading on the New York Stock Exchange. Staples slipped $1.06 to $23.50 on Nasdaq.

The Federal Trade Commission voted 4 to 1 to seek a preliminary injunction in Federal District Court against the proposed 1,000-store combination. The companies promised a vigorous fight against an equally determined agency.

"The fact is that in those communities where Staples faces competition from Office Depot, prices are significantly lower than where it does not," said William Baer, director of the FTC's bureau of competition. He said if the two chains merged, "competition will be reduced or eliminated and consumers will pay higher prices."

The FTC said the companies compete in about 40 cities and that a merger would reduce competition in California, Florida, Illinois, Kentucky, Maryland, Michigan, New Jersey, New York, North and South Carolina, Ohio, Oregon, Pennsylvania, Tennessee, Virginia, Washington, Indiana, Utah and in Washington D.C.

According to the chains, that is wrong. They argue that prices will stay low because the superstores compete with many others in the market for office supplies. They also say the merger would create new efficiencies.

"Cost savings will be passed on to (consumers) in the form of lower prices," said Staples Chairman Thomas Stemberg. The presidents of both chains promised to "vigorously contest the Federal Trade Commission's attempt to block the merger of the two companies."

If that struggle takes place, it will be a rare event in the world of trust-busting. Pharmacy giant Rite Aid Corp. abandoned its attempt to acquire Revco pharmacies one week after the FTC voted in 1996 to block the deal.

Office Depot and Staples will make their case before a Federal District Court judge some time in the next month or two, after the FTC seeks a temporary restraining order to prevent a quick merger, and an antitrust expert said the outcome is up in the air.

"Preliminary injunctions in merger cases are always hard fought and generally unpredictable," said Don Baker, of Baker & Miller PLLC in Washington. "If the government has some eye-catching documents they might well have a 50-50 chance of getting a preliminary injunction or a tough 'hold-separate' order."
A 'hold separate' order requires merged companies to operate their enterprise separately until litigation ends.

That litigation will move on its own special track, before an FTC administrative law judge, whose decision will be reviewed by the FTC -- all of which will take at least 13 months and is subject to more appeals.
One analyst said that if the merger cannot be completed, Office Depot would be more poorly positioned than Staples to handle the fallout.

Ursula Moran, an analyst for Sanford Bernstein in New York, said Staples was moving ahead, as reflected in excellent fourth-quarter earning results. By contrast, she said, Office Depot had not done as well.

"Momentum at Office Depot has been difficult since the merger announcement," she said, noting staff had been allowed to drift away in anticipation of functions being transferred to Staples headquarters after the merger.
"If the merger really does get called off, the first task for Depot is to go out and hire more people," she said.
Analysts had expected that if the deal went through, Staples and Office Depot would have to divest some stores. The third office superstore player, OfficeMax, was considered a likely buyer.
But others said there was no reason for OfficeMax to ease the way for its competitors to merge.
"There's not a lot of incentive for OfficeMax to be constructive in this process," said Christopher Vroom, at Alex. Brown in New York.
